title: TB5-04535
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Appellants, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, are citizens of Nigeria, and appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated April 9, 2015, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellants, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, are citizens of Nigeria, and appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated April 9, 2015, rejecting their claims for refugee protection. The Appellants are submitting new evidence and are requesting an oral hearing; in the event the RAD does not set aside the RPD determination, the Appellants request that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD.

The RPD hearing was held on March 30, 2015 and a decision rendered on April 9, 2015. The RPD found that the Appellants were not convention refugees or persons in need of protection because they could avail themselves of an IFA in Nigeria.

Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) confirms the determination of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

The Appellants are minors who fear returning to Nigeria on account of Boko Haram, because of their Christian religion. The Appellants' parents are in Canada as are two other siblings. The Appellants' father left for Canada on a student visa in August of 2014 leaving the rest of the family in Nigeria. The Appellants' mother and their other two siblings arrived in Canada via the United States in January of 2015. A month later, the Appellants came to Canada directly from Nigeria as unaccompanied minors. The Appellants' refugee claim was heard jointly with that of their mother and the other two siblings. For whatever reason, the Appellants' father did not make a refugee claim. The RPD heard all of the claims in one hearing and made one decision for all of the claimants. All of the refugee claimants relied on the written and oral testimony provided at the RPD hearing by the Appellants' mother. The Appellant XXXX also provided some testimony.

Because the Appellant's mother and the other two siblings entered Canada from the United States, they were precluded from appealing to the RAD because of the third safe country rule. The Appellants, having arrived directly from Nigeria are appealing their RPD decision directly to the RAD.

The RAD finds that the recent Federal Court decision, in Huruglica,1 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal such as the RAD to decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal. Justice Phelan states in paragraphs 54 and 55 of the foregoing decision: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision. [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error".

While there has been some conflict in the case law from the Federal Court regarding the standard to be applied by the RAD when reviewing RPD decisions, Justice Martineau, in Alyafi,2 has said that, in the face of this conflict, the Federal Court should allow the RAD to apply either approach as long as the question of the scope of the appellate review of the RPD's decisions has not been settled by a final judgment by the Federal Court of Appeal or the Supreme Court of Canada.

Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its own assessment of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection and will consider only the issues raised by the Appellant. New Evidence Documentary Evidence
The Appellants submitted new evidence in the form of a psychological report from XXXX XXXX, dated May 20, 2015, with respect to the Appellants' mother.

The document is a psychological assessment of the Appellants' mother who is not an appellant in this appeal. The RAD has read the document and finds that its contents are neither pertinent nor significant to the Appellants of this particular appeal for it describes the psychological assessment of the Appellants' mother who is not part of this appeal. In the event that the RAD is wrong on this point, it will also conduct an analysis under s.110(4) of the IRPA.

The RAD's analysis of the admissibility of the proposed new evidence must begin first with the test set out in s. 110(4) which states: On appeal, the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.
As with respect to the first test, the date of the document is May 20, 2015 which is after the date that the RPD rendered its decision.

With respect to the second test, the RAD finds that, although the written report was generated after the date of the RPD decision, the information provided in the report did not arise after the RPD decision and was readily available to the Appellants' prior to the RPD rendering its decision.

After having reviewed the contents of the Appellants' submitted documents, the RAD finds that this evidence was reasonably available to the Appellants prior to the rejection of their claim and that the Appellants have provided no persuasive explanation of why they could not reasonably have tendered that evidence prior to the rejection of their claim. The RAD finds that the new evidence does not meet the test of s. 110(4) of the IRPA.
As no new evidence was tendered in this appeal, the RAD must proceed without a hearing; the application for an oral hearing is denied.
The RPD found that the determinative issues in these claims were credibility and an Internal Flight Alternative. Issues Raised by Appellant
paragraphs.heading_before: ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: The Appellant raises the issues of credibility, IAF and the application of the Gender Guidelines. Gender Guidelines

Counsel for the Appellants argues that the RPD failed to apply the Board's Gender Guidelines. The Gender guidelines are not explicitly mentioned by the RPD in its decision. However, the RAD had the opportunity to listen to the recording of the RPD hearing and finds that, in fact, the RPD did apply the Gender Guidelines during the hearing. All of the claimants were represented by an experienced counsel who was given an opportunity to ask questions and make submissions. The RPD provided ample time for the Appellants' mother to reply to the questions, and explained the questions when requested to do so by the Appellants' mother.

The RPD found that the Appellants' mother was a credible witness; accepted their identity as Christians and the fact that they had experienced mistreatment and discrimination as a result of their Christian faith while living in the Northern area of Nigeria. However, the Board found that the claimants had a viable IFA in cities in Southern Nigeria. In its written submissions, the Appellants' counsel states: " The Board accepted the testimony given by XXXX and XXXX and made no adverse credibility findings; the sole issue was the internal flight alternative.(IFA)3" IFA

As stated earlier, the original claimants included the two Appellants, their mother and two other siblings. With the exception of the Appellants, all of the other claimants arrived in Canada via the United States and thus were precluded from filing an appeal to the RAD. The majority of the testimony was provided by the Appellants' mother including her testimony of whether the cities of Port Harcourt, Lagos and Ibadan in Southern Nigeria were viable IFA alternatives for the claimants.

In assessing an IFA, the RAD must apply a two-pronged test cited in Rasaratnam4 suitably modified to take account of s. 97 of the IRPA. 1) The Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA. 2) Moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for him to see refuge there

Both prongs must be satisfied to find that the Appellant has an IFA. The burden of proof rests with the Appellants to show that they do not have an IFA. The finding of an IFA must be based on a distinct evaluation of a region for that purpose, taking into account the Appellant's identity. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option. An Appellant cannot be required to encounter great physical danger or to undergo undue hardship in traveling there or staying there.5
The RAD finds that there is a reasonable and viable IFA available to the Appellants in Port Harcourt or Benin City in Nigeria.

The RAD considered whether the RPD erred in its application of the first prong of the Rasaratnam6 test. The Appellants' mother stated that she fears returning to Nigeria because of the activities of Boko Haram against Christians. Although she testified that this problem is being experienced all over the country, the RAD finds that the Appellants have failed to provide any convincing evidence that they would suffer harm or persecution at the hands of the agents of persecution if they were to relocate to any of the cities suggested as an IFA. In fact, during the RPD hearing, the Appellants' mother was asked if she could freely practice her Christian faith in the south and she replied that she could. The RAD agrees with the RPD finding that there was no serious possibility that the Appellants would be persecuted or that they would be subject, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture, or to a risk to their lives, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment in the proposed IFA.

The RAD also considered whether the RPD also assessed the second prong of the Rasaratnam7 test: reasonableness of the IFA. The RAD considered the reasonableness of the proposed IFAs. The test for reasonableness is whether it would be unduly harsh to expect the claimant to move to another, less hostile part of the country before seeking protection abroad, as per Thirunavukkarasu.8 This requires an evaluation of the conditions in the IFA, as well as the condition of the Appellants or similarly-situated persons. Thirunavukkarasu sets a very high threshold for what makes an IFA unreasonable in all the circumstances. The hardship associated with dislocation and relocation is not the kind of undue hardship that renders an IFA unreasonable.9 However, it is not enough for the Appellant to say that he or she does not like the weather there, or that he or she has no friends or relatives there, or that he or she may not be able to find suitable work there.10

The RPD found that it would not be unreasonable for the Appellants to find refuge in the proposed IFA. The RAD notes that the RPD questioned the Appellants' mother in regard to the proposed IFA. The Appellants' mother testified that the main reason as to why the family cannot relocate in these cities is because, coming from the North of the country, the family would be treated as indigenous people in the Southern part of the country. Counsel provided extensive submissions with respect to the treatment of individuals from the Northern Part of Nigeria who relocate to the Southern part of the country11.

The RAD notes however, the United Kingdom Home Office Country of Origin Report for Nigeria12 states that the Nigerian constitution provides for the right to travel within Nigeria. The report also states that internal relocation to escape ill-treatment from non-state agents is almost always an option and, in the absence of exceptional circumstances, it would not be unduly harsh for any individual to internally relocate.

The evidence in the record, in particular, the United Kingdom Home Office Operational Guidance Note for Nigeria indicates that Nigeria is a large country and internal relocation will generally be a viable option for those who fear, or who have experienced ill-treatment at the hands of non-state agents.

The RAD considered the Appellants' ethnic background, language, religion and gender as potential barriers to the reasonableness of the re-location to the IFA cities. The RAD agrees that if the Appellants were to relocate to the south, they would be considered as indigenous individuals. The information provided by the Appellants' counsel with respect to the treatment of indigenous people in Southern Nigeria does indicate that some ethnic mistreatment against indigenous individuals does take place and that there has been tensions and even some discrimination against indigenous people, the RAD finds that these conditions experienced by indigenous people in Southern Nigeria would not jeopardize the life nor the safety of the Appellants. The documentary evidence indicates that Appellants are unlikely to face discrimination due to their ethnicity in either of the proposed IFA cities.

The RAD notes that the Federal Court has established a very high threshold for the unreasonableness test. A decision by Justice Zinn cites the Thirunavukkarasu13 decision that indicates that, in order for an IFA to be unreasonable: ...it requires nothing less than the existence of conditions which would jeopardize the life and safety of the claimant in traveling or temporarily relocating to a safe area...This is in sharp contrast with undue hardship resulting from loss of employment, loss of status, reduction in quality of life, loss of aspirations, loss of beloved ones and frustration of one's wishes and expectations.14

Based on this jurisprudence, and based on the general concerns put forward regarding the reasonableness of the IFA (lack of employment, being cut-off from family), the RAD finds that the RPD did not err in finding that the IFA was reasonable for the Appellants as argued by counsel.

The RAD finds that the RPD carefully considered the totality of the evidence before it in regards to the reasonableness of an IFA. Its finding that the proposed IFA was reasonable was transparent and considered the particular situation of the Appellants. For these reasons, the RAD finds that the RPD did not err in finding that the Appellants had a reasonable IFA in the proposed cities.

Given the finding above, that the Appellants have an IFA in Nigeria, the RAD finds that the Appellants do not face a serious possibility of persecution there and also finds that their removal to Nigeria would not subject them personally to a risk to their lives, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture.
The RAD finds that there is an IFA for the Appellants, and since IFA is a determinative issue, the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

Pursuant to ss. 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD. (signed) "Pasquale A. Fiorino" Pasquale A. Fiorino July 22, 2015 Date 1 Huruglica, Bujar v. M.C.I. (F.C., no.
